newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani rupee seen weakening again in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani rupee seen weakening again in 1997.

text.p: The Pakistani rupee is likely to weaken further in 1997 after losing over 17 percent of its dollar value this year because of high inflation, a huge trade deficit and low foreign exchange reserves, analysts said.

"The rupee will continue to depreciate, though at a lower pace, as all factors that put pressure on the rupee value are still there," Maqsood Ahmed, vice president of the private Muslim Commercial Bank, told Reuters.
Pakistan's liquid foreign exchange reserves, excluding gold, rose to $788 million on December 12 from $745 million on December 5, but Maqsood said the rise was temporaray.
"The rise is not because of higher foreign exchange earnings but because of higher short-term borrowing which will further exert pressure on Pakistan's external account balance," he said.

Fahim Ahmad, a forex analyst at Banque Indo Suez, said the rupee was likely to depreciate by another 10 to 12 percent in 1997 in the face of an unfavourable balance of payments position and purchasing power parity, or inflation.
"The double digit growth in inflation and persistently high trade deficit justifies a 10 to 12 percent devaluation by the end of 1997," Ahmad said.

The Federal Bureau of Statistics said the consumer price index rose 11.18 percent year-on-year in November from 10.48 percent in November 1995, but Fahim said most analysts believed the actual figure could be anywhere between 15 to 20 percent.

"If compared to the U.S. rate of inflation, which at the moment is around 2.0 to 2.5 percent, a 10 to 12 percent devaluation of the rupee against the dollar (in 1997) would be a conservative estimate," he said.
Pakistan's trade deficit fell to a provisional $1.511 billion in the first five months of fiscal 1996/97 (July-June) from $1.745 billion in the year-ago period.
Analysts said the gap at the end of the fiscal year was unlikely to be very different from last year's deficit of $3.666 billion.
They said the 17.14 percent erosion of the rupee, including a 7.86 percent devaluation on October 22, had helped boost exports but had done little to bring down the trade deficit.

A foreign banker, who asked not to be named, said the six-month forward rate for the dollar in the interbank market was still around 43 rupees, reflecting expectations that the rupee will depreciate by at least nine percent in 1997.
